grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: la llave → las llaves; la silla blanca → las sillas blancas; está → están; tiene → tienen.

tables.caption: es · son; está · están; tiene · tienen

La puerta del armario está abierta.
La puerta de la sala está cerrada.
Ana y Luis tienen dos sillas blancas.

grammar.note_en:
A plural refers to more than one person or thing. Spanish usually adds -s after an unstressed vowel: llave → llaves, “key → keys”; silla → sillas, “chair → chairs”. A noun ending in a consonant adds -es here: papel → papeles, “paper → papers”. Keep the original word and add the ending; do not add an apostrophe. Dos llaves means “two keys”, tres sillas “three chairs” and cuatro sillas “four chairs”. Uno means “one”; before a masculine singular noun it has the shorter form un, and with a feminine noun it is una.

Articles change with number as well as gender. El libro becomes los libros, “the book → the books”; la llave becomes las llaves, “the key → the keys”. Los goes with masculine plural nouns and las with feminine plural nouns. Dos and the other numbers do not take the place of the noun’s gender: dos llaves still refers to feminine keys.

Adjectives agree with the noun they describe. La llave corta means “the short key”; las sillas blancas means “the white chairs”. Blanca has feminine plural blancas: tres sillas blancas, “three white chairs”. Negro becomes negra with silla: una silla negra, “a black chair”. The contrasts largo/corto (“long/short”), viejo/nuevo (“old/new”) and abierto/cerrado (“open/closed”) are separate meanings, not grammatical rules about colour or size. A white chair can be old or new; an open door can be large or small. Here a folded chair is described as cerrada and an unfolded chair as abierta.

A verb also changes when its subject is plural. Es becomes son for a plural description: Son dos llaves means “They are two keys”; Tres sillas son blancas means “Three chairs are white”. Está becomes están for location or state: Las dos llaves están fuera de la caja means “The two keys are outside the box”. Ana y Luis have a plural subject even though each person is named individually. Ana y Luis tienen dos sillas blancas means “Ana and Luis have two white chairs”; tienen contrasts with singular tiene. The same pattern appears in mira/miran (“looks/look”), abre/abren (“opens/open”), entra/entran (“enters/enter”). These are third-person forms, for named people or things; forms for “I” and “you” come next.

Descriptions and states use the copula, a linking verb: son describes the keys or chairs; están says where things are or whether a door or chair is open. La puerta está cerrada means “The door is closed”. La puerta está abierta means “The door is open”. This does not yet teach an action meaning “close”; the forms describe the resulting state. The blue key opens the cupboard, which changes its door from cerrada to abierta. The room door remains closed.

Otro/otra means “another” or “the other”, according to context; otra silla is “another chair”, la otra puerta “the other door”. With an article, mismo/misma means “same”: la misma llave, “the same key”; el mismo nombre, “the same name”. Number and gender still agree: las otras tres means “the other three”, referring to chairs already named. Uno and una can also stand without a repeated noun: Una está abierta means “One is open”, referring to a chair. These shorter phrases work only when the surrounding text makes the missing noun clear.

The table phrases mean: la llave / las llaves, “the key / the keys”; una silla blanca / dos sillas blancas, “a white chair / two white chairs”; el papel / los papeles, “the paper / the papers”. Son dos llaves means “They are two keys”; La puerta del armario está abierta means “The cupboard door is open”; La puerta de la sala está cerrada means “The room door is closed”. Tres sillas son blancas means “Three chairs are white”.
